paper.title: A Fast, Minimal Memory, Consistent Hash Algorithm

program.how: written for ounce-core from the paper's Figure 1 and its explanation (64-bit LCG seeded with the key, next jump floor((b+1)/r)); own mixing function to generate keys; own ln() and exp-free code; no third-party code copied
program.target: static freestanding aarch64 Linux ELF, run with `ounce-core run-elf` (a few double multiplications and divisions, no libm, built with -ffp-contract=off)

claims_checked: Monotonicity: going from n to n+1 buckets a key either stays or moves to the new bucket n; 0 violations in 4000000 (key, n) steps (20000 keys, n = 1..200)
The paper's example that growing from 10 to 12 buckets moves 1/6 of the data: 33325 of 200000 generated keys moved (0.1666), tolerance 0.01 absolute, fixed in advance
The paper's example that adding a bucket to 1000 moves about 0.1% of the keys: 486 of 500000 moved (range 400 to 600 fixed in advance), all of them to the new bucket

The analysis in 'Performance Analysis': the expected number of loop iterations is 1 plus the sum of 1/i for i = 2..n, and below ln(n)+1: the measured mean over 200000 keys is within 2% of that sum and below ln(n)+1 for n = 2, 3, 10, 100, 1000, 100000 (6 of 6)

expected_values_source.what: the text of the paper: Figure 1 (the algorithm), the 10 to 12 shards and 1000 buckets examples in the Introduction and Key Distribution sections, and the Performance Analysis section
expected_values_source.note: the paper's three-key table (k1, k2, k3 over 1 to 14 buckets) does not state its keys, so it cannot be reproduced; its Figure 2 standard error 0.00000000764 and Figure 4 timings are measurements on the authors' data and hardware and are not compared. The tolerances are sampling tolerances for the generated key sets, fixed before the first run.

negative_control: built with -DNEG=1 (random value taken from key>>32 instead of key>>33) 35596 monotonicity violations appear, 0 of 6 iteration-count rows agree with the analysis, the 1000 to 1001 move is no longer only to the new bucket, and the program exits 1
not_checked: the bucket-size standard error of Figure 2 (7.64e-9), which needs far more keys than a Tier-3 run, and the comparison with Karger et al.'s algorithm
execution time, memory requirements and the cache-effect measurements (Figures 3 to 5)
keys wider than 64 bits (the paper says to hash them first)
Tier-4 and native ARM64 execution (the native comparison is x86-64)
what_a_pass_means: this program, run on ounce-core, shows jump consistent hash behaves as the paper states for the properties and examples listed. It does not reproduce the paper's measurements.
